To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the isotype of the antibodies involved in immune complexes has a profound effect on the capacity of the complexes to activate complement, (2) epitope density is a critical determinant of the capacity of immune‐complex‐bound antibody to activate complement, and (3) the amount of complement bound to the complexes is a critical determinant for their capacity to bind to CR1.

the complement‐fixation activity and binding to CR1 of immune complexes are determined by the isotype and epitope density of the antibody, the antigen/antibodies ratio and the pathway of complement fixation.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the interaction between the human immune system and the complement system.
the interaction between antibody and antigen and how the resulting immune complex interacts with complement and with the C3b/C4b receptor of erythrocytes.

the study of the role of immunological and non‐immunological factors in the pathogenesis of immune complex‐mediated diseases, with the aim of developing a better understanding of the disease mechanisms and to provide the basis for the design of new therapeutic agents.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the capacity of an antibody to activate the classical pathway is a reflection of its capacity to bind complement and that, for IgM, IgA and IgG2, the capacity to activate complement is a function of the antigen/antibodY ratio and of epitope density.
complement‐fixing immune complexes are best formed when antigen/antibodies ratio and epitope density are high and when IgG1, IgG3 or IgA antibodies are used.
the complement‐fixating activity of immune complexes is determined by the antibody isotype, the epitope density, the antigen/antibodY ratio, and, possibly, the age of the complexes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the isotype and epitope density of the antibody are the most important factors determining the capacity of immune complex to fix complement and bind to CR1.
IgG3, IgG1, IgG2, IgM, and IgA have different capacities for activating complement, and that this is dependent on epitope density and on antigen/antibodies ratio.

the isotypes and subclasses of antibody and epitope density and ratio are important determinants of the capacity of immune‐complex‐formed antigen to activate the complement system, which in turn is a major factor in the ability of these immune complexes to be deposited in tissues and to cause damage.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the complement‐fixation capacity of immune complexes is highly dependent on antibody isotype, epitopic density and antigen/ antibody ratio.

complement fixation is not a simple function of antibody and antigen concentration, and it is important to know what the antibody and antigen concentrations are, and what the epitope densities on the antigen are.

complement activation by immune complexes depends on the isotype and epitope density of the antibodies, the epitope density of antigen, the antigen/antibodies ratio and the complement pathway activated.
